Section 138 of the Act prescribes the offence whereby a dishonoured cheque is returned unpaid by the bank. Dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds is currently a punishable offence that carries imprisonment for a term of one year or with a fine which may extend to twice the amount of the amount in accordance with Section 138.The provision is sui generis in itself since it prescribes the offence and penalty for the offence as well. Section 141 of the Act stipulates that in cases where the offence has been committed by a company, every person who was in charge and responsible to regulate the conduct of the business of the company are vicariously liable with the company, for the said the offence. In other words, since the companies are juristic entities, it is the director(s) behind the curtains, who are responsible for the decisions. Thus, this provision expressly applies the principle of vicarious liability of the directors along with the company.

Significantly, the procedure for taking cognizance of cases under the Act is distinct from the procedure established under the Cr PC. The underlying reason behind the same is that Section 138 of the Act is person-specific. The court cannot take cognizance under Section 138 in the absence of a complaint in writing that is made by the payee or the holder of the cheque. Thus, even the Cr PC has to give way to the procedure established under the Act.

To buttress the legislative scheme as addressed hereinabove, it is a settled position of law that in accordance with Section 141 of the Act, it is sine qua non that the accused company is arraigned as a party along with all of its directors who were in charge and responsible for the company at the time the cheque was issued.3

Curable Defect v/s Incurable Defects

If viewed from the macro level, it would reveal that the accused company could often take advantage of such loopholes and become recalcitrant in their behavior that could lead to an abuse of the law. Therefore, this part seeks to address the solutions apropos the research problem.

♦ Curable Defects

Pertinently, the error committed by the learned trial court is a procedural irregularity or a procedural defect that is curable at any subsequent stage before the trial concludes. Therefore, in simpler terms, the error of the trial court is a curable defect. Moreover, curable defects should not be permitted to impede the genuine case of the complainants. This finds strength from the judgment of the Supreme Court in Haryana State Cooperative Supply & Marketing Federation Ltd. v. Jayam Textiles4, wherein it was observed that procedural defects and irregularities which are curable should not be allowed to defeat substantive rights or to cause injustice.

Significantly, this curable defect should also not impede the case of the complainant merely due to the error of the learned trial court. If permitted, it could prove to be a fatal blow that would fly in the face of the complainant's legitimate case. Therefore, in the interest of justice, it would be apposite that the learned trial court treats the same as a curable defect on the immediate next date of hearing.

♦ Curing the Procedural Defect

After having categorized the pitfall of the learned trial court in not issuing summons to the company but rather only to the authorized signatory as a procedural defect that is curable, organically, the next question that would arise for consideration would be related to the ways and means of curing this defect.

Significantly, the CrPC does not encapsulate any provision that permits the complainant to amend the complaint. This is further problematic since if the learned trial court did not issue summons to the accused company, it would be in direct violation of Section 141 of the Act. Thus, this part will specifically cover the legality and procedure of amending the complaint that has been filed under Section 138 of the Act.

Significantly, the Supreme Court in S.R. Sukumar v. S. Sunaad Raghuram5 held that despite the absence of a provision allowing an amendment to a complaint under Cr PC, the same is permissible if it relates to a simple infirmity which is curable by means of a formal amendment. It was held that such an amendment would be covered under Section 190(1)(a) of the Cr PC. However, this permissibility of an amendment is subjected to the degree of prejudice to the other side. Significantly, apart from weighing the prejudice that could be caused to the accused, another factor that must be noted concerns the extent of avoiding any multiplicity of litigation. If denying an amendment is likely to give birth to another set of proceedings, it could be equally disastrous bringing the position back to square one.

Therefore, whilst permitting an amendment, the courts must be conscious about two indispensable aspects viz., (i) whether or not the amendment could cause any prejudice to the other side and (ii) whether denying the amendment could lead to another set of litigation. These two factors could plausibly answer and clear the mist around substantial aspects.

The banks asserted first charge over the secured assets under SARFAESI, while EPFO claimed statutory priority under section 11(2) of the Provident Fund Act.

The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant and directed deposit of an interim amount without examining the competing claims of priority, particularly in the absence of Axis Bank as a party. The Supreme Court held that, since Axis Bank had realised substantial sale proceeds and was now impleaded before the Court, it was necessary for the High Court to first examine the inter se priority of charges between EPFO and the secured creditors in accordance with section 11(2) of the PF Act and section 35 of the SARFAESI Act. 9. Notice issued to partners is deemed notice to firm and partners are jointly and severally liable u/s 138 of NI Act

Dhanasingh Prabhu v. Chandrasekar [2025] 176 taxmann.com 443 (SC)

In the present case, the Supreme Court examined whether a complaint under section 138 read with section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, is maintainable against partners of a partnership firm when the statutory notice was issued only to the partners and not separately to the firm, and the firm itself was not initially named as an accused. The appellant-complainant had advanced a loan to the respondents, who were partners of a firm, and a cheque issued from the firm's account towards discharge of the debt was dishonoured. The High Court had quashed the complaint on the ground that the partnership firm was neither served with statutory notice nor made a party to the proceedings, and therefore the requirements of section 141 were not satisfied. Reversing the High Court's view, the Supreme Court held that a partnership firm is not a separate juristic entity distinct from its partners but only a compendious name for the partners, who are jointly and severally liable for the acts of the firm. It was observed that, unlike a company where liability of directors is vicarious, the liability of partners is direct and joint. The Court further held that even in the absence of the firm being named as an accused, proceedings against the partners are maintainable, and any such defect is curable by permitting the firm to be **impleaded** at a later stage. Accordingly, the Supreme Court set aside the impugned order of the High Court and restored the complaint.

An Overview of Section 138 under N.I. Act

Negotiable Instruments have long been used in the business world as one of the simplest ways to move capital. Until 1988, there was no effective legislative mechanism to prevent individuals from issuing checks without adequate funds in their account, nor was there any severe penalty for doing so. For instance, a legal responsibility arose from the non-payment of checks. To secure the check's drawee, it was decided that cheque dishonour should be considered a criminal offence. Banking, Public Financial Institutions, and Negotiable Instruments Laws (Amendment) Act, 1988 added Sec.138 to 142 for that reason. This was accomplished by having the drawer responsible for fines if the check bounced due to a lack of funds, with sufficient protections in place to deter abuse of the truthful drawer. However, it was later discovered that the courts were unwilling to resolve the proceedings in a timely and efficient fashion. The loopholes were filled in by the amendment of 2002, which resulted in the passage of the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2002. The provisions of sections 143 to 147 were included, and the provisions of sections 138, 141, and 142 were changed.

This amendment act aimed to control the growing business, exchange, commerce, and industrial activities and encourage greater financial vigilance. Also, to protect creditors' trust in the cheque box. The Hon'ble SC in the matter of Modi Cements Ltd. v. Kuchil Kumar Nandi held that "The object of Chapter XVII, containing Sections 138 to 142, is to promote the efficacy of banking operations and to ensure credibility in transacting business through cheques."1

Under Sections 118 and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, there are presumptions in favour of the receiver of the cheque that it was drawn to discharge debts or liabilities. It is, however, rebuttable, and the victim will refute it by cross-examination without having to reach the witness box. The complainant is also responsible for proving that the check was given for a properly enforceable debt or liability. The burden on the accused in such a situation will be heavier than in proceedings under section 114 of the Evidence Act. The operation of notification is deemed to have been effected until notice is submitted by registered mail to the proper addressee of the cheque, as stated in Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, and Section 114 of the Evidence Act, 1872. The drawer, on the other hand, is free to refute this assumption as per N. Paraeswaran Unni v. G. Kannan2. Section 139 provides a requirement that the holder of a cheque collects the cheque in discharge, in full or in part, of any debt or other obligation until the execution of the cheque is admitted, It was held in Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa3. Cheques with no date or post-dated cheques are often given. In Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar4, the Supreme Court held that if a signed blank cheque is willingly handed over to a payee for any payment, the payee is free to fill in the balance and other information. This will not invalidate the check on its own.

In the case of Kusum Ingots and Alloys Ltd v. Pennar Peterson Securities Ltd5, the Supreme Court found out the basic ingredients of the crime as contemplated under Sec.138 of the act that, "an individual must have drawn a check on a bank account that he maintains for transfer of a certain sum of money to another person from that account for the discharge of some debt or other liability; the cheque was issued to the bank within six months of the date on which it was drawn, or within the validity limit of the cheque, whichever comes first; According to RBI guidelines, the validity duration of Cheques, Demand Drafts, Pay Orders, and Banker's Cheques has been shortened from six to three months as of April 1, 2012, from the date of the instrument. The bank returns the check as outstanding. either because the sum of money in the account is inadequate to honour the cheque or because it reaches the amount arranged to be charged by the account under a bank agreement; within 30 days of receiving details from the bank about the return of the cheque as outstanding, the payee or issuer of the cheque makes a case for reimbursement of the said sum of money by sending a note in writing to the drawer of the cheque; within 15 days of receiving the said note, the drawer of the cheque fails to allow delivery of the said sum of money to the payee or the holder of the cheque in the proper course of the cheque."

4. Legal Framework of the Dishonour of Cheque

(a) The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Sections 138 to 147 - To ensure promptitude and remedy against defaulters and to make sure credibility of the holders of the negotiable instrument, a criminal remedy of penalty was inserted in the Act, in form of the Banking, Public Financial Institutions and Negotiable Instruments Laws (Amendment) Act, 1988 that inserted sections 138 to 147 in the Act, which were further modified by the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2002.

The issue of dishonour of cheque is dealt with under sections 138 to 147 that provide for remedies and various forms of punishment in case of dishonour of cheque. Section 138 deals with the dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account. It provides that a person shall be punishable for two years imprisonment or with fine, if the cheque issued by drawers is returned by the bank unpaid. The cheque must be issued in discharge of whole or part, of any debt or other liability.

The presumption in favour of holder is drawn against the drawer and in favour of the holder under section 13911 of the Act that cheque is received by the holder in discharge of whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. Further, section 1401 2 of the Act provides that a person drawing a cheque cannot take up the defence that when he drew the cheque he had no idea that his credit balance in the account was insufficient.

The offences by the companies have been dealt with under section 1411 3 (1) of the Act, which provides that if a person committing an offence under the section is a company, every person who at the time when offence was committed, was in-charge of, and was responsible to, the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly.

Section 14214 of the Act states that the cognizance of an offence can be taken under section 138 upon a complaint in writing which must be made within one month by the payee or holder in due course from the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to section 138.15 If there is no proof of service of the notice of demand as required under section 138, the prosecution of the drawer is not permissible.16

The summary trial of cases has been provided under section 1431 7 of the Act. Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974) (in short ‘code’), all offences under this Chapter shall be tried by a Judicial Magistrate of the first class or by a Metropolitan Magistrate and the provisions of sections 262 to 265 of the Code shall, as far as may be, apply to such trials. Further, under section 14418 of the Act, mode of service of summons has been provided. Section 14519 deals with the evidence on affidavit. Section 14620 provides that bank’s slip is prima facie evidence of certain facts and section 14721 states that all the offences punishable under the Act shall be compoundable.

Fixed deposit - Joint account

A fixed deposit in the joint names of two persons is nothing but a joint account which, as the name itself suggests, is payable on the expiration of the agreed period. The fixed deposit receipt is merely a written acknowledgement by the bank that it holds a certain sum to the use of its customers. The bank is thus a debtor to the account holders in respect of the amount deposited a debt which is repayable by the bank to the account holder with interest on the expiry of an agreed period. [Anumati v. Punjab National Bank [2005] 126 Comp. Cas. 322 (SC)]

The debt in the form of fixed deposit receipt is that of the bank to the joint account holders and the bank cannot set off a debt due from one of the joint account holders against such a joint debt (Nath Bank Ltd. v. Sisir Kumar Sarkar AIR 1954 Cal. 303). In Hirschorn v. Evans (Barclays Bank Ltd., Garnishee) (1938) 2 KB 801 (L), it was held that inasmuch as the debt which the bank owed was not a debt due to the husband alone, but to him jointly with his wife, it could not be attached to answer the judgment against the husband.

a person is penalised by virtue of his status, even if he has not committed any offence or omission. The modern concept of penal laws with reference to public, social welfare legislations or economic laws, contradicts the traditional penal theory which insists upon identifiable mens rea identifiable conduct, identifiable victim, identifiable harm.

Sherras v. De Rutzen [1895] 1 QB 918 Wright, J., found that there are three classes of cases where the Legislature normally enacts absolute prohibition : (1) One is a class of acts which, in the language of Lush J. in Davis v. Harvey (Law Rep. 9 QB 433) are not criminal in any real sense, but are acts which in the public interest are prohibited under a penalty. Several such instances are to be found in the decisions on the Revenue Statutes, Adulteration Acts, Games Acts etc.;

(2) Another class comprehends some, and perhaps all, public nuisances : Reg v. Stephens (Law Rep 1 QB 702) where the employer was held liable on the indictment for a nuisance caused by workmen without his knowledge and contrary to his orders;

(3) Lastly, there may be cases in which, although the proceeding is criminal in form, it is really a summary mode of enforcing a civil right : see per Williams and Willes JJ. in Modern v. Porter [7 C.B (N.S.) 641; 29 LJ (M.C. 213], as to the unintentional trespass in pursuit of game; Lee v. Simpson (3 C.B. 871) as to unconscious dramatic piracy and Hargreaves v. Diddams (Law Rep. 10 QB 582), as to a bona fide belief in a legally impossible right to fish.

The Bombay High Court, after quoting Sherras v. De Rutzen, observed as follows in Mayuri Pulse Mills v. Union of India [1996] 86 Comp. 121 (Bom.) :

“Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, can be said to be falling either in the class of acts which are not criminal in a real sense, but are acts which in the public interest are prohibited under the penalty or those where although the proceedings may be criminal in form, they are really only a summary mode of enforcing a civil right.”

5.22D-7h MENS REA AND VICARIOUS AND STRICT LIABILITY - It is well-settled that the strict criminal liability of companies, partnership firms, or legal persons is in a class by itself and poses problems peculiar to them. Since a legal person is a fiction of the law and does not exist in actuality, the issue of vicarious liability of the office bearers through whom a company or a partnership firm or association of persons must necessarily act, comes to the fore.1 Strict vicarious liability is somewhat an exception to the general rule of direct personal culpability and is a modern development through statutory provisions. That there can be such vicarious criminal liability by legislative mandate is no longer in dispute. Nevertheless steeped as we are in the basic principles of criminal jurisprudence that mens rea must be an ingredient of an offence and both the act and intent must concur to constitute a crime, it requires some effort to accept whole-heartedly the legislative mandate of vicarious criminality even in the absence of either of the aforesaid ingredients.

Vicarious liability ‘is a necessary doctrine for the proper enforcement of much modern legislation—but it is not one to be extended.1 Whether one person will be held responsible for the acts of another is a matter of construction in each case. Regard must be had to the object of the statute, the words used, the nature of the duty laid down, the person upon whom it is imposed, the person by whom it would in ordinary circumstances be performed and the person upon whom the penalty is imposed.2

If the doctrine of vicarious liability is held to apply, a person subject to a statutory duty to which a penal sanction is attached who chooses to delegate the performance of that duty to another person (usually but not necessarily an employee), will nevertheless be himself liable for breaches of that duty by his delegate. In many cases his delegate’s ‘knowledge’ will be imputed to him.3

But it is equally well-settled that if the servant, at the time of the accident, is not acting within the course of his employment, but is doing something for himself, the master is not liable. There is a presumption that a vehicle is driven on the master’s business and by his authorised agent or servant but presumption can be met.4

Upon filing the requisite documents along with the complaint, and once the Accused acknowledges the cheque or its contents, the Complainant's burden is substantially fulfilled. In this case, the Accused demonstrated through certified Income Tax Returns that the Complainant lacked the financial capacity to advance the alleged loan amount, thereby successfully rebutting the statutory presumption. The Admission qua the signature of a "cheque" is sufficient to trigger section 139 of the NI Act . The Supreme Court in Bir Singh v. Complainant/Payee has no onus to prove the financial capacity at the threshold.

In proceedings under Section 138 of the NI Act, the Complainant is not required to establish their financial capacity at the initial stage. Once the drawer admits to signing the cheque, the statutory presumption under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act operates in favour of the Complainant, presuming the existence of a legally enforceable debt. The onus is not on the Complainant at the threshold to prove their financial wherewithal to make the payment in discharge of which the cheque was allegedly issued. Only if an objection is specifically raised in the reply notice or any pleading that the Complainant lacked the financial position to advance the claimed loan amount, would the Complainant be required to bring cogent material indicating financial capacity and actual advancement of the loan.

Recently, in Ashok Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh25, the Appellant/Complainant had advanced a loan to the Accused, who in discharge of the debt, issued a cheque. When presented, the cheque was dishonoured with the endorsement "payment stopped by drawer." A legal notice was sent within, but the Accused neither replied nor made payment. The Trial Court and Appellate Court convicted the Accused under Section 138 of the NI Act after finding the debt legally enforceable. However, the High Court reversed this decision, holding that the Complainant failed to prove his case because he did not disclose bank account details, the date of withdrawal, or the specific date when the cheque was obtained. The Supreme Court found this approach fundamentally erroneous. The Accused had admitted signing the cheque but claimed it was lost, though the intimation about the lost cheque was suspiciously sent to the police only a year after the cheque was presented. Further, the Accused had not raised the defence of the Complainant's lack of financial capacity in his reply notice. In fact, no reply was given to the statutory notice at all.

6.3 Twin contingencies under section 138 to be interpreted strictly - The two contingencies mentioned in section 138 have to be interpreted 'strictly or literally'. The expression "amount of money…. is insufficient" in section 138 is a genus and dishonour for reasons such "as account closed", "payment stopped", "referred to the drawer" are only species of that genus. Just as dishonour of a cheque on the ground that the account has been closed is a dishonour falling in the first contingency referred to in section 138, so also dishonour on the ground that the "signatures do not match" or that the "image is not found", which too implies that the specimen signatures do not match the signatures on the cheque would constitute a dishonour within the meaning of section 138 of the Act. The Court has said that on the parity of the decision in the earlier cases where it has been held that if after issue of the cheque, the drawer closes the account then it must be presumed that the amount in the account was nil hence, insufficient to meet the demand of the cheque. A similar result can be brought about by the drawer changing his specimen signature given to the bank or in the case of a company, the company changing the mandate of those authorized to sign the cheques on its behalf. Such changes or alteration in the mandate may be dishonest or fraudulent and that would inevitably result in dishonour of all cheques signed by the previously authorized signatories. According to the Court, there is no qualitative difference between a situation where the dishonour takes place on account of the substitution by a new set of authorized signatories resulting in the dishonour of the cheques already issued and another situation in which the drawer of the cheque changes his signatures or closes the account or issues instructions to the bank not to make the payment. So long as the change is brought about with a view to preventing the cheque being honoured the dishonour would become an offence under section 138 subject to other conditions prescribed being satisfied. In situations where mismatch in signatures is inadvertent – never intended by the drawer or where the authorized signatory gets changed in the ordinary course of business of a company, the question whether or not there was a lawfully recoverable debt or liability for discharge whereof the cheque was issued would be a matter that the trial Court will examine, having regard to the evidence adduced before it and keeping in view the statutory presumption that unless rebutted the cheque is presumed to have been issued for a valid consideration.

Does Criminal Liability has Solved the Problem?

6. The criminal liability under section 138 has not solved the problem of cheque bouncing and did not develop faith in this credit instrument among the people who widely use it. Our judiciary has played a crucial role by imposing strict liability when the cheque is dishonoured but it does not work effectively and still the cheques are getting dishonoured. It is evident from the fact that Courts are overburdened due to the complaints of dishonour of cheques in spite of law in this regard.

(a) The Act - A failure - It is sadly submitted that the Act is a failure; numerous factors have contributed to this failure. The structural flaws intrinsic in the Act caused its failure, more than anything else, but the larger reason of failure is socio-culture.

The activity which the Act was enacted to remove is still rampant. In other words, people still choose to gather cash in the discharge of obligations owed to them in preference to cheque. It is general place to get that people still hold large amount of cash in settlement of financial obligations and in consummation of commercial activities. The foremost reason for the preference for cash is a lack of confidence in the use of cheques. This lack of confidence is primarily due to the continuing prevalence of dishonoured cheques.

(i) Socio Cultural Impediment - The failure of the Act has more sociological and cultural bases than structural defects inbuilt in the Act. Indians do have extremely small regard for the imperatives of discharging their financial obligations. They think nothing erroneous in issuing a cheque for the reason of discharging their financial obligations that they know will be dishonoured on presentation for insufficiency of funds in their bank accounts. This is a constituent of the encompassing widespread corruption that damages the foundation of Indian society. They don’t file a complaint for being issued a dishonoured cheque in the court, but would rather find other means of getting back debts owed to them by the drawers of the cheque.

There is a dearth of reported cases of the offence created in the Act and by implication, of prosecution of cases under the Act. There is an urgent need to amend the Act.

(ii) Adequacy of the Penalty - The punishment provided by the Act has become dreadfully low and reflects very little significance about limiting the criminal behaviour to which the Act is committed. Only two years imprisonment has been provided which seems to be very less in view of the wrong.

(iii) Cognizance of offences - The procedure provided under section 142 of the Act is not friendly and viable because it provides that the Court will take cognizance of offence or complaint only in writing. Its merely cumbersome formality. The Court should take the cognizance of offences or complaint in oral also as provided under section 200 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973.

In this decision, the SC's observations are to the following effect:-

"37. The court's jurisdiction to interpret a statute can be invoked when the same is ambiguous. It is well-known that in a given case, the court can iron out the fabric but it cannot change the texture of the fabric. It cannot enlarge the scope of legislation or intention when the language of the provision is plain and unambiguous. It cannot add or subtract words to a statute or read something into it, which is not there. It cannot rewite or recast legislation. It is also necessary to determine that there exists presumption that the legislature has not used any superfluous words. It is well settled that the real intention of the legislation must be gathered from the language used…."

(b)

In this decision, the observations on interpretation are:-

"The interpretative function of the court is to discover the true legislative intent. It is trite that in interpreting a statute, the court must, if the words are clear, plain, unambiguous and reasonably susceptible to only one meaning, give to the words that meaning, irrespective of the consequences. Those words must be expounded in their natural and ordinary sense. When the language is plain and unambiguous and admits of only one meaning, no question of construction of statute arises for the Act speaks for itself. Courts are not concerned with the policy involved or that the results are injurious or otherwise, which may follow from giving effect to the language used. If the words used are capable of one construction only then it would not be open to the courts to adopt any other hypothetical construction on the ground that such construction is more consistent with the alleged object and policy of the Act. In considering whether there is ambiguity, the court must look at the statute as a whole and consider the appropriateness of the meaning in a particular context avoiding absurdity and inconsistencies or unreasonableness, which may render the statute unconstitutional".

India, from the past 3 decades have been imprisoning defaulter, in cases of dishonoring of Cheque, nevertheless having an international obligation of not doing so. Article 11 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, of which India too is a party, explicitly outlaws the construct of imprisoning the person for not fulfilling or failing to discharge their contractual obligation; the rationale behind it is that imprisoning such parties will serve no social purpose even after attaching all their property or assets have been attached and possessed by their creditor. Recently, the Center has proposed to decriminalize the dishonoring of cheque coupled with other minor offences. The rationale given for such proposal was that criminal liabilities for minor offences act as deterrents, and this is perceived as one the major reasons impacting business sentiment and hindering investments both from domestic and foreign investors; eventually, this will facilitate unclogging the court process as according to a 213th Law Commission Report, there is about 40 lakh pending dishonor of cheque cases. Recently, the Confederation of All India Trader (CAIT) penned down a letter to the Finance Minister urging to address the issue of rising menace of dishonored cheque hampering the credibility of the crucial payment instrument in the trade ecosystem. The letter in addition to this also cited an observation made by erstwhile Justice Adarsh Kumar Goel, observing that the impugned offence must be decriminalized to lift the burden from the judiciary system1. Whether the cheque dishonor should be decriminalized or not, has become a contemporary issue across India. As to the other developed nations, a cheque is a civil offence. Many civilized nations have already done away with the idea of putting their citizens behind the bars because of their inability to discharge their contractual debts. In India, Section 138 of the Negotiable Instrument Act, 1888 deals with the actual denotation of Dishonour cheque and also imposes criminal liability upon a person who unknowingly/knowingly dishonors cheque. Back in 1988, through amendment, the civil wrong was transformed into an offence and thereby was criminalized. The amendment was based on the report on the committee on banking laws by Dr. Rajamannar, submitted in 1975, which suggested, inter alia, penalizing the act of dishonour. Cheque Dishonour followed by default in payment after a demand notice became punishable under Section 138 with imprisonment or fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque or both.2

Key Ingredients of section 138

In Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan3, the court read Section 138 of the Act with section 177 to 179 of CrPC, 1973. It was observed that the offence under Section 138 can be completed only with the concatenation of the following ingredients:

Cheque should be issued to discharge any debt or liability, wholly or partly, through a live account.

Cheque should be presented within six months (now three months according to the latest directive of RBI) or before its validity expires.

The cheque issued should have been returned by the bank because of the insufficient amount of money in the drawer's account or exceeds the credit arrangement to the payee or holder by the bank itself.

The payee or holder within thirty days should have issued a notice to make a demand for the payment of the said amount since the bank returned the cheque unpaid.

The drawer of such cheque fails to make payment to the payee or holder in the due course, within 15 days from the receipt of that demand.

From the expiry of those 15 days, the payee or holder is allowed to file a complaint in writing, within a period of one month.

Reasons to decriminalise the dishonor of Cheque

Apart from the violation of international conventions, we are still using that mode of payment in which the majority of strong economies are now discouraging it and moving towards a less-cash society by opting for other better alternatives. The rationale behind decriminalising includes the following noteworthy points:

(1)

Unequal treatment among debtors – Section 138 of Negotiable Instrument Act bifurcates and discriminates, and provides different treatment to different debtors. For instance, if a millionaire company goes bankrupt in India, Directors take the shield of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and hence they are not sent to jail for taking the company into bankruptcy. Then why an individual, who commits the same offence, is booked with a criminal charge and sent to jail?4

(2)

Contravenes Contract Law – For instance, in cases of post-dated cheque, a party cannot unilaterally terminate the contract, even if the contract allows so, as there would always be a fear of initiation of a criminal proceeding for cheque bounce against them.

(3)

Falsity - On account of an advocate or agent

A person cannot escape liability on the ground that he is mere signatory of the statement or an instrument for delivering account or statement as the documents were prepared by his advocate or agent. There may be a situation which could arise, as pointed out in Clixby v. Pountney (Inspector of Taxes) [1969] 72 ITR 340 (Ch.D.), when a person cannot be held guilty on that basis but such cases are rare.

If all these conditions are fulfilled, the banker who pays is not only discharged from all liability on the instrument but can also debit the person on whose account the payment was made with the amount so paid. Now, an amendment has been made by adding two sub-sections as follows : "(2) Where the cheque is the electronic image of a truncated cheque, any difference in apparent tenor of the electronic image and the truncated cheque shall be a material alteration and it shall be the duty of the bank or the clearing house, as the case may be to ensure the exactness of the apparent tenor of the electronic image of the truncated cheque while truncating and transmitting the image.

(3) Any bank or a clearing house which receives a transmitted electronic image of a truncated cheque, shall verify from the party who transmitted the image to it, that the image so transmitted to it and received by it, is exactly the same."

Dishonour of cheques and criminal proceedings

8. Chapter XVII (sections 138 to 142) of the NI Act deals with the case of dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds in the accounts and penalties. As per the provisions of section 138, a person who has committed an offence shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with fine, which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque or with both. The punishment prescribed under the Act has not been found to be sufficient enough to act as a deterrent. Under the amendment the punishment of imprisonment has been increased to two years from the existing one year. Similarly the time for making of demand by the payee or holder has been increased from the present fifteen days to thirty days.

Under section 142, cognizance of any offence under section 138 can be taken only if a complaint is made in writing by the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque as the case may be within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the provision to section 138. Such a restriction puts the payee to a disadvantage as there may be reasons beyond the control of the payee for not being able to file the complaint within the prescribed period. It is now provided that the cognizance of a complaint may be taken by the Court after the prescribed period, if the complainant satisfies the Court that he had sufficient cause for not making a complaint within such a period.

Presently, the court follows the procedure prescribed under the Code of Criminal Procedure wherein the complainant’s evidence (pre-summons evidence) is to be recorded before the complaint is admitted or notice is issued to the accused. It causes a lot of delay in disposal of cases. The fact of dishonour of cheque being simple and verifiable by a third party i.e., bank, the return of the cheque by the bank due to reasons as prescribed under section 138 shall be the conclusive proof of admitting and issue of notice to the accused. The recording of pre-summons evidence of the complainant in such cases leads to delay. The amendment proposed is to incorporate new sections providing that an affidavit filed by the complainant along with a copy of the bank’s memo returning unpaid cheque and copy of the notice to the drawer shall be taken as the conclusive proof for admitting the petition and issue of notice to the accused. Thus, the procedure of Code of Criminal Procedure of recording evidence of the complainant before admitting the petition is to be dispensed with. For service of summons, a new provision is to be made providing for service of summons by the court through speed post or short listed/empanelled private couriers.

In this case, the appellant, the Managing Director of Surana Power Limited, relying on P. Mohanraj (supra), submitted that the expression “legal action or proceeding in respect of any debt” in Sections 96 and 101 is wide enough to include Section 138 proceedings, as the moratorium extends to any legal proceeding relatable to recovery of debt. He also contended that the objective of the moratorium under Part II and Part III is the same i.e. to prevent depletion of assets and provide breathing space and accordingly the reasoning in P. Mohanraj (supra) should equally apply to personal insolvency. However, the High Court rejected the same, holding that proceedings under Section 138 of the NI Act are not debt recovery proceedings and therefore do not fall within the scope of the moratorium under Section 96. The Court further observed that Section 138 is a penal provision providing for imprisonment and fine, and hence cannot be equated with recovery proceedings.

The Supreme Court undertook a detailed examination of the nature of cheque dishonour proceedings and expressed reservations about the reasoning adopted in P. Mohanraj (supra).

The Bench observed that proceedings under Section 138 cannot be viewed merely as mechanisms for debt recovery. According to the Court, the main purpose of Section 138 is to maintain public confidence in commercial transactions by attaching penal consequences to cheque dishonour. Therefore, the criminal aspect of the provision is not secondary to the compensation aspect. While the Court observed that the purpose under both Part II and Part III is to provide breathing space to restructure assets and liabilities, however, the Court was also conscious that certain liabilities are not protected by the moratorium even though their consequence might deplete the debtor’s assets; the rationale being that the moratorium is intended to shield the debtor from recovery actions and civil claims, and not from the consequences of criminal misconduct. Accordingly, the mere possibility that a criminal proceeding may ultimately result in a financial burden on the debtor cannot, by itself, bring such proceedings within the ambit of the moratorium.

Further, the Court also explained that proceedings under Section 138 have two separate elements:

1.

Compensatory element, which aimed at ensuring payment of the cheque amount and compensation to the complainant, therefore, should be within the moratorium.

2.

Criminal element, which aimed at punishing the offence of cheque dishonour through penal consequence, and Moratorium under Part III of IBC does not apply to criminal proceedings.

In view of the above, the Court observed that while the insolvency moratorium may impact the compensatory aspect, it does not necessarily bar or suspend the criminal prosecution.

Since this understanding appeared to differ from the reasoning in P. Mohanraj (supra), which had treated Section 138 proceedings as primarily compensatory and therefore subject to moratorium, the matter was referred to a larger Bench for authoritative determination.

Concluding remarks:

The decision in P. Mohanraj (supra) brought clarity to the law by holding that proceedings under Section 138 of the NI Act against a CD are covered by the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC. At the same time, the Court made it clear that this protection is available only to the CD and not to its directors, signatories, or other persons responsible for the company's affairs. This position was thereafter consistently followed by courts.

However, in Dineshchand Surana (supra), the Supreme Court revisited the nature of Section 138 proceedings and questioned the basis of the reasoning adopted in P. Mohanraj (supra). The Court observed the 2 tier aspects of Section 138 proceeding, i.e. (a) compensatory aspect, and (b) a criminal aspect. This led the Court to raise a significant question as to if the moratorium is intended to protect the debtor's assets and therefore affects the recovery aspect, should it also stop the criminal prosecution?

The SARFAESI Act provides a general punishment of imprisonment upto one year or with fine, if any person contravenes or attempts to contravene any provision of Act. [section 29 of SARFAESI Act].

4.5-1 Offences by company

If offence is committed by a company (the term includes partnership firm or association of individuals), every person who was in-charge of or was responsible to affairs of the Company/firm is deemed to be guilty. Normally, a Managing Director (partner in case of firm) or other person specially authorised is deemed to be in-charge. However, such person can prove that offence was committed without his knowledge or he had taken due care to prevent the offence [section 33(1) of SARFAESI Act].

In addition, if it is proved that the offence in relation to Company is committed with consent or connivance of, or due to neglect on part of any director, manager or Secretary or other officer of Company, such person shall be deemed to be guilty [section 33(2) of SARFAESI Act].

Difference between provisions of section 33(1) and 33(2) of SARFAESI Act is that in former case, the person-in-charge is deemed to be guilty and burden of proof is on him to prove that he had no knowledge; while in later case, burden of proof is on prosecution to prove that offence was committed with knowledge or connivance of the director, manager, secretary or other officer.

Culpability of company under Income-tax Act/Wealth-tax Act 11.10-9 What should be disturbing indeed is the retrograde lead taken by the law-makers, to the relief of the Prosecutors and the Judiciary alike though, so far as the Income Tax Act and the Wealth Tax Act are concerned: a sub-section (3) has been added to sections 278B and 35HA, respectively, that came into force from 1st October, 2004, by the Finance Act (No.2) 2004, reading-"Where an offence under this Act has been committed by a person, being a company, and the punishment for such offence is imprisonment and fine, then, without prejudice to the provisions in sub-section (1) or sub-section (2), such company shall be punished with fine and every person referred to in sub-section (1) or the director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company referred to in sub-section (2), shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished in accordance with the provisions of the Act". From the point of accountability of companies to the society at large with their great resource-backed potential for mischief it is unfortunate, the trend set in law of attribution of culpability to the company as such in our country is just to let it go with fine and nothing more to it. This development seems to be the result of the majority decision of the three member bench in Asstt. Commissioner v. Velliappa Textiles 2003 AIR SCW 5647, saying that a company cannot be prosecuted if the provision in law is punishment by imprisonment only. It is unfortunate because even in the present day modern social order it is difficult to assume that the King can do no wrong or that all of His wrongs are off in a money-wash, and a company and its directors being far less privileged than a King at any rate, some other alternative provision in law, may be business inhibitory in nature and commensurate to the seriousness of the economic offence involved at least for a short run of time, ought to be attributable to the company that stigmatises the directors automatically, in the interest of natural justice to curb the obsession with public mischief for private profit in disguise.

11.10-9a The trend has been stalled by Supreme Court - However, the later decision of Supreme Court in Standard Chartered Bank v. Directorate of Enforcement [2005] 275 ITR 81/145 Taxman 154 to the effect that there is no immunity to the companies from prosecution merely because the prosecution is in respect of offences for which the punishment prescribed is mandatory imprisonment, seems to be rational and correct, both in itself and constitutionally.

Background of ‘Standard Chartered’ majority verdict

11.10-10 The 2:1 decision of the three Judge Bench in Velliappa’s case is said to be in line with the Law Commission recommendation made in its 41st and 47th Reports suggesting amendments to the Acts relating to economic offences and the IPC to say that offences punishable with only imprisonment or imprisonment and fine means only fine when the offender is a company or corporation, leading to an amendment proposed to the IPC in 1972 that had lapsed. The majority decision in Velliappa’s case was based on the Act provision being mandatory imprisonment plus fine, leaving no choice to the Court to impose only fine in lieu of imprisonment, leading to the conclusion that a company cannot be prosecuted for such offences until the Act is amended as was done in Australia, Belgium, Canada, France, Netherlands and the EU, on the footing that it is not Court’s function "to repair the blunders that are to be found in legislation. They must be corrected by the Legislature": Bristol Guardians v. Bristol Waterworks Co. (1914) AC 379. The minority judgment given by Mathur J. in the said case was that the Court would be shrinking from its responsibility of imparting justice by the conclusion that a juristic person like a company cannot be sent to jail and therefore it is free from prosecution even for serious offences which only attract mandatory imprisonment in law. The verdict of the 3-Judge Bench in ANZ Grindlays Bank Ltd. v. Directorate of Enforcement [2005] 58 SCL 350 (SC) doubted the correctness of the majority verdict in Velliappa’s case; and in Standard Chartered case, cited above, a 5-Judge Bench gave the verdict with 3:2 majority that companies or corporations cannot go scot-free having committed serious offences, and it also cannot be the intention of the Legislature to grant blanket immunity in that fashion, and in that view of the matter it was taken that discretion is given to the Court to impose prison sentence or fine in such cases, over-ruling the Velliappa precedent.

'Offences by companies.—(1) Where a person committing contravention of any of the provisions of this Act or of any rule, direction or order made thereunder is a company, every person who, at the time the contravention was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to, the company, for the conduct of the business of the company as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the contravention and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly.

The rigour and stringency of the rule is tempered by holding that such a person on whom the vicarious liability has been thrust may cast off such a liability if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence. The burden of proof is clearly laid upon such a person and such is the rule of evidence which reverses the ordinary mandate of criminal liability that the burden of establishing the prosecution lies on the prosecution. 5.22D-7l MENS REA IN RESPECT OF IMPUTED LIABILITY - Criminal liability could be an imputed liability as is found in section 278B of the Income-tax Act, 1961 or in a provision of Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940; Industrial Disputes Act, Essential Commodities Act, 1955 etc. The liability is to be imputed to high managerial officers (who at the time of the commission of offence, were in charge of and responsible to the conduct of the company’s business), because the company cannot be executed or punished with corporal punishment. The person is liable because his action is the very action of the company itself and is charged as a person-in-charge of and responsible to the conduct of the company’s business, and not in his individual capacity. The prosecution case cannot rest on the ground that the person concerned is personally responsible for the commission or omission of the act. The prosecution has to be foisted upon him because he has been in charge of and responsible to the conduct of the business of the company. The person is not said to be prosecuted independently of his character as being the person-in-charge and responsible. Thus, once it is found that there had been contravention of the provisions of a statute by a company or a firm, the persons who are in charge of the business and are responsible for its conduct cannot escape liability, unless they prove by leading evidence that contravention took place without their knowledge or in spite of diligence exercised by them.2

The person ‘in charge’ must mean that the person should be in overall control of the day-to-day business of the company.3 The Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Pratap Chand4 considered the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. The three respondents being the partners of the firm, Mafatlal & Co., and the firm itself was charged for offences under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. The Chief Metropolitan Magistrate found respondents 1 and 3, that is, one of the partners of the firm, guilty under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and sentenced respondent 1 to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 500; in default, to suffer simple imprisonment for three months. Respondent 2 was acquitted of these two offences as the Magistrate found respondent 1 and not respondent 2 to be in charge of the business of the firm. All the respondents were acquitted of the offence. The appellant preferred an appeal before the High Court of Karnataka from the order of acquittal of respondent 2 of the offence.The High Court summarily dismissed the appeal. The partner of a firm is also liable under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act to be convicted for an offence committed by the firm if he was in charge of and responsible to the firm for the conduct of the business of the firm or if it is proved that the offence was committed with the consent or connivance of, or was attributable to any neglect on the part of the partner concerned. In the present case, respondent 2 was sought to be made liable on the ground that he along with the first respondent was in charge of the conduct of the business of the firm. Since it was found that respondent 1 and not respondent 2 was in overall control of day-to-day business of the firm, respondent 2 was held not liable to be convicted merely because he had the right to participate in the business of the firm under the terms of the partnership deed. In another case, Sham Sunder v. State of Haryana1, the Supreme Court held that there was no evidence that all the partners were conducting the business of the firm and, thus, all cannot be indicted for the offence under section 10 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The argument that in a firm each partner is a representative of the other was rejected by holding that it is relevant in a civil liability and not in criminal liability and that there is no vicarious liability in criminal law unless the statute takes that also within its fold.

The person who is liable to be proceeded and punished for imputed liabilities should be the one who was in charge of, and was responsible to, the company for the conduct of the company’s business at the time of commission of the offence. The managing director of the company from his very designation implies both the control and command of the affairs of such a company and equally a statutory liability to the company for responsible conduct of its business. It is a compendious term which signifies both control of and responsibility to the company both in ordinary parlance and by virtue of the provisions of the Indian Companies Act. Similarly, in the case of manager, from the very nature of his duties, it can be safely inferred that he would undoubtedly by vicariously liable for the offences, vicarious liability being an incident of an offence.2

Even the Court had noted the fact that the assessee and the wife were living separately since 10-10-1979. Thus, the whole case of the Assessing Officer was based on suspicion, surmises and conjectures and he had made additions in respect of assets found from the premises of the wife and from locker held by her and additions could not be sustained in law. - Asstt. Joint liability - Criminal Act

As a general principle in a case of criminal liability it is the primary responsibility of the person who commits the offence and only that person who has committed the crime can be held guilty. By introducing section 34 in Indian Penal Code the Legislature laid down the principle of joint liability in doing criminal act. The essence of that liability is to be found in the existence of common intention connecting the accused leading to the doing of a criminal act in furtherance of such intention. Thus, if the act is the result of a common intention then every person who did the criminal act with the common intention would be responsible for the offence committed irrespective of the share which he had in its perpetration. [Ramesh Singh v. State of Andhra Pradesh [2004] 20 ILD 77 (SC)]. As observed by the Supreme Court in Ashok Kumar v. State of Punjab AIR 1977 SC 109, the existence of common intention is an essential ingredient of section 34. It is not necessary that the acts of the several persons charged with commission of an offence jointly must be the same or identically similar. The acts may be different in character, but must have been actuated by one and the same common intention (see Raju Pandurang Mahale v. State of Maharashtra AIR 2004 SC 1677; [2004] 4 SCC 371). That section is applicable even when no injury has been caused by the particular accused himself (Ch. Pulla Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh AIR 1993 SC 1899)

Liability of partner, karta or managing trustee - Where an offence under this Act has been committed by a taxable person being a partnership firm or a Limited Liability Partnership or a Hindu Undivided Family or a trust, the partner or karta or managing trustee, as the case may be, shall be deemed to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly and the provisions of section 137(2) shall apply mutatis mutandis to such persons - section 137(3) of CGST Act.

No punishment if offence without knowledge or when due diligence exercised - Nothing contained in this section shall render any such person liable to any punishment provided in this Act, if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he had exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence - section 137(4) of CGST Act.

Offences by companies

55. (1) If the person committing an offence under this Code is a company, every person who, at the time the offence was committed was in charge of, and was responsible to the company for the conduct of business of the company, as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly:

63. Where an employer is charged with an offence under this Code, he shall be entitled upon complaint duly made by him, to have any other person whom he charges as the actual offender, brought before the court at the time appointed for hearing the charge; and if, after the commission of the offence has been proved, the employer proves to the satisfaction of the court—

(a)

that he has used due diligence to enforce the execution of this Code; and

(b)

that the said other person committed the offence in question without his knowledge, consent or connivance,

that other person shall be convicted of the offence and shall be liable to the like punishment as if he were the employer and the employer shall be discharged from any liability under this Code in respect of such offence:

Possession involves animus

Possession involves animus and corpus. If there is animus, it is immaterial whether the possession is actual or constructive or physical or mediate or immediate or direct or indirect or exclusive, joint or concurrent (see Narendra Nath Mozumdar v. State AIR 1951 Cal. 140). When a property is in the possession of a person’s wife, clerk or servant of that person, it is in the person’s possession (section 27 of the Indian Penal Code)

Person- in-charge and responsible to the company

In the case of a company and particularly a public limited company the person-in-charge of the company and responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company are the board of directors. In other words every director of a company is a person in-charge of the company and responsible to the company for the conduct of its business (Ashok Leyland Finance Ltd. v. R. S. Aggarwal (2003) 10 Scale 1000). But every director is not responsible for an offence. In Smt. Katta Sujatha v. Fertilizers and Chemicals Travancore Ltd. [2002] 7 SCC 655, the Supreme Court observed that a person could be a party to the policy being followed by a company and yet not be in-charge of the business of a company or that a person may be in-charge of a company but not in overall charge or that a person may be in-charge of only some part of the business of the company. The Supreme Court laid down that not all the directors of a company will be responsible for the conduct of the business of the company. This has been so held despite the general law that a company is governed by the board of directors. Apart from being a director, the accused director also need to have been involved either in the management of the specific part of the business of the company relating to the offence or he should be in actual overall control of the business and not merely a member of the board of directors or responsible for the conduct of the business of the company by virtue of being a director of the company only [see Everest Advertising (P.) Ltd. v. State [2005] 128 Comp. Cas. 787 (Delhi)]

Person-in-charge means that the person should be in control of the day- to-day business of the company [See Girdharilal Gupta v. D. N. Mehta AIR 1971 SC 2162 and State of Karnataka v. Pratap Chand [1981] 128 ITR 573 (SC)]. The Supreme Court in Sham Sunder v. State of Haryana [1990] 67 Comp. Cas. 1 observed that all the partners of a firm are not liable for an offence committed by the firm irrespective of whether they were running the business or not, and that it would be a travesty of justice to prosecute all the partners and ask them to prove that the offence was committed without their knowledge.

A person is said to be responsible to the company for the conduct of the business if he has the control and authority over the conduct of the business and the duty to take care in respect thereof. Lord Diplock observed in Tesco Supermarkets Ltd. v. Nattras (1972) AC 153 (HL), as follows:

"in my view, therefore, the question : what natural persons are to be treated in law as being the company for the purpose of acts done in the course of its business, including the taking of precautions and exercise of due diligence to avoid the commission of a criminal offence, is to be found by identifying the natural persons who by the memorandum and articles of association or as a result of action taken by the directors, or by the company in general meeting pursuant to the articles, are entrusted with the exercise of the powers of the company."

personnel. The term ‘officer’ is wide enough to include the Secretary or Assistant or Deputy Secretary or Accountant, Official Liquidator, Golcha Properties (P.) Ltd. v. P.C. Dhadda [1980] 50 Comp. Cas. 175 (Raj.). [See, discussion in Chapter 10-Corporate Capacity]. Indemnification by the company is void unless acquitted or discharged or judgment given in favour of the accused director [Section 201]. 26.26-7-1 WHERE THE DIRECTORS ARE HELD LIABLE - Whether the directors are ‘principal officers’ or agents for purposes of Income-tax Act can only be determined on evidence, Shyam Sunder Jalan v. State [1977] 47 Comp. Cas. 61 (Cal.), but if a person is shown as a director in a return, he is an officer, H.H. Marthanda Varma v. Registrar of Companies [1988] 64 Comp. Cas. 125 (Kar.). In a case where the ROC has issued the notice to all the directors in respect of a default committed by a company under sections 166/168 and 220, but with no response from any of them, prosecution may be launched against all of the directors as ‘officers in default’, Asstt. Registrar of Companies v. Southern Machinery Works Ltd. [1986] 59 Comp. Cas. 670 (Mad.). In respect of offences under the Minimum Wages Act, each and every director is liable to be prosecuted, Hari Charan Singh Dugal v. State of Bihar [1989] 66 Comp. Cas. 449 (Pat.). The liability to be prosecuted extends even after retirement if a person who was a director at the time of commission of the offence and therefore an officer in default - Anita Chadda v. Registrar of Companies [1998] 8 SCL 304 (Delhi).

26.26-7-2 WHERE THE DIRECTORS HELD NOT LIABLE - In respect of offences under the Companies Act, only those of the officers who are knowingly and wilfully guilty of the offence can be punished, Consolidated Pneumatic Tool Co. (I) Ltd. v. Addl. Registrar of Companies [1989] 65 Comp. Cas. 259 (Bom.). Thus, where the company accepted deposits in excess in contravention of section 58A of the Act, a director who was neither the managing director nor a whole-time director nor was involved in the day-to-day affairs of the company nor even a shareholder, could not be said to be ‘an officer in default’, H. Nanjundiah v. V. Govindan, Registrar of Companies [1986] 59 Comp. Cas. 356 (Bom.). In any case, the liability does not attach by the mere fact of one being a director: there should be either an averment that the director is ‘an officer in default’ in terms of section 5 of the Act, or an allegation in the complaint that the director or the managing director was responsible for the conduct of the company’s business, and if that averment is absent the complaint is not maintainable, Hindustan Development Corpn. Ltd. v. Kushan Chand Bader [1998] 94 Comp. Cas. 384/15 SCL 1 (Raj.); V.B. Sivalingam Chettiar v. Labour Officer [1986] 59 Comp. Cas. 701 (AP); Ramachandra Manilal Kotla v.State of Gujarat (1998) 30 CLA 313 (Guj.).

It is vehemently submitted that the ingredients of section 138 of the NI Act are not satisfied, and therefore, the High Court ought to have quashed the criminal complaint against the appellant. 3.1 It is further submitted by the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant that, in the facts and circumstances of the case, even section 141 of the NI Act shall not be applicable as the cheque was issued by a private individual.

4. The present appeal is vehemently opposed by the learned counsel appearing on behalf of respondent No. 1 - original complainant.

4.1 It is submitted that the liability to pay the debt towards the professional bill was the joint liability of both the accused as the complainant represented both the accused and, therefore, as rightly observed and held by the High Court, section 141 of the NI Act shall be applicable.

4.2 It is submitted that when the Trial Court issued the summons against the appellant for the offence punishable under section 138 r/w section 141 of the NI Act after having come to the conclusion that a prima facie case has been made out, the High Court has rightly refused to quash the criminal complaint. 4.3 It is further submitted that as the cheque was issued towards discharge of legal liability of both the accused and thereafter when her husband issued the cheque, the High Court has rightly refused to quash the complaint.

5. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the State has supported the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court.

6. We have heard learned counsel appearing on behalf of the respective parties at length, considered material on record and also considered the averments and allegations in the complaint. It emerges from the record that the dishonoured cheque was issued by original accused No. 1 - husband of the appellant. It was drawn from the bank account of original accused No. 1. The dishonoured cheque was signed by original accused No. 1. Therefore, the dishonoured cheque was signed by original accused No. 1 and it was drawn on the bank account of original accused No. 1. The appellant herein-original accused No. 2 is neither the signatory to the cheque nor the dishonoured cheque was drawn from her bank account. That the account in question was not a joint account. In the light of the aforesaid facts, it is required to be considered whether the appellant herein - original accused No. 2 can be prosecuted for the offence punishable under section 138 r/w Section 141 of the NI Act?

7. On a fair reading of section 138 of the NI Act, before a person can be prosecuted, the following conditions are required to be satisfied:

(i)

that the cheque is drawn by a person and on an account maintained by him with a banker;

(ii)

for the payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability; and

(iii)

the said cheque is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account.

Therefore, a person who is the signatory to the cheque and the cheque is drawn by that person on an account maintained by him and the cheque has been issued for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability and the said cheque has been returned by the bank unpaid, such person can be said to have committed an offence. Section 138 of the NI Act does not speak about the joint liability. Even in case of a joint liability, in case of individual persons, a person other than a person who has drawn the cheque on an account maintained by him, cannot be prosecuted for the offence under section 138 of the NI Act. A person might have been jointly liable to pay the debt, but if such a person who might have been liable to pay the debt jointly, cannot be prosecuted unless the bank account is jointly maintained and that he was a signatory to the cheque.

8. Now, so far as the case on behalf of the original complainant that the appellant herein - original accused No. 2 can be convicted with the aid of section 141 of the NI Act is concerned, the aforesaid has no substance.

Section 138, read with section 139, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency etc., of funds in account - Whether for initiation of prosecution under section 138, a prior statutory notice is mandatorily required to be given to drawer, to make good payment of amount mentioned in cheque and only when drawer receives a notice and fails to make payment within time provided by Statute, does dishonour become an offence - Held, yes - A complaint was filed against accused under section 138 by complainant on ground that accused had taken friendly loan from complainant and a cheque issued by accused in favour of complainant was dishonoured on presentation - It was noted that subject cheque, copy of which had been placed on record, was signed only by late husband of accused - Although conceded that cheque was issued from a joint account but subject cheque did not bear signature of accused - Whether thus, criminal complaint filed against accused was clearly an abuse of process of law - Held, yes - Whether thus, instant petition by accused filed under section 482 of Cr.P.C seeking quashing of criminal complaint filed under section 138 was to be allowed and consequently, criminal complaint against accused was to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 7, 8  11]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Where a complaint under section 138 was filed against accused on ground that cheque issued by her to discharge her loan liability had been dishonoured, in view of fact that said cheque was issued from a account jointly held by accused and her late husband but subject cheque did not bear signature of accused but of her late husband, criminal complaint filed against accused was clearly an abuse of process of law and was to be quashed

Concededly, in the instant, section 141 of the NI Act is not attracted as the offence is not committed by a company. The petitioner has been impleaded in her individual capacity. The liability under section 138 NI Act arises on account of dishonour of cheque issued for the discharge, in whole or in part of any debt or other liability. Further, for initiation of prosecution under section 138 NI Act, a prior statutory notice is mandatorily required to be given to the drawer, to make good the payment of the amount mentioned in the cheque and only when the drawer receives a notice and fails to make the payment within the time provided by the Statute, does the dishonour become an offence. [Para 7]

In the instant case, the issue whether the statutory notice was issued, in view of the factual situation wherein the complainant states that the accused refused to accept notice while the accused states that no such notice was received, is a matter of trial. However, the complaint case must fail owing to a more fundamental issue. The subject cheque, copy of which has been placed on record, was signed only by late husband of accused, i.e., 'A'. Although it is conceded that the cheque was issued from an account jointly in the name of the 'A' and accused however, it is a matter of fact that the said cheque is not signed by the accused. [Para 8]

In view of the above, the criminal complaint filed against the accused is clearly an abuse of process of law and the same is liable to be quashed and set aside. Consequently, the instant petition is allowed and the criminal complaint against the accused is quashed. Pending application is also disposed of as infructuous. [Para 11]

FACT: The accused and complainant had been friends and had known each other for about 15 years. Subsequently, on account of some financial difficulty, the accused took a friendly loan of Rs. 20 lakh from the complainant with a promise to repay the same once her financial crisis was over. The accused, in discharge of her debt/liability, issued a cheque. The said cheque, when presented for encashment was dishonoured with the remarks 'stop payment'.

Thus, a complaint under section 138 was filed against accused. By way of instant petition filed under section 482 Cr.P.C. read with article 227 of the Constitution of India, the accused was seeking quash of Complaint Case instituted under section 138 pending before Metropolitan Megistrate. According to accused although the cheque was issued from a joint account but the subject cheque did not bear her signature and thus, the complaint filed against her was not maintainable.

HELD: Concededly, in the instant, section 141 of the NI Act is not attracted as the offence is not committed by a company. The petitioner has been impleaded in her individual capacity. The liability under section 138 NI Act arises on account of dishonour of cheque issued for the discharge, in whole or in part of any debt or other liability. Further, for initiation of prosecution under section 138 NI Act, a prior statutory notice is mandatorily required to be given to the drawer, to make good the payment of the amount mentioned in the cheque and only when the drawer receives a notice and fails to make the payment within the time provided by the Statute, does the dishonour become an offence. [Para 7]

from which the complaint case emanated, was neither drawn by the petitioner nor was issued from her bank account nor was it bearing her signatures. Petitioner further submitted that as the petitioner was not a joint-account holder, she could not be made liable for the offence under section 138.

HELD: As per section 138, if the drawer of the cheque fails to make the payment on receipt of the legal notice, he is liable to be prosecuted under section 138. [Para 9] In the instant proceedings, admittedly, the impugned cheque has not been issued/drawn by the petitioner and it has been issued by her brother from his bank account wherein the petitioner is not an account holder. As such, in view of the provisions of section 138, the petitioner, under the instant circumstances, cannot be held liable for something not concerning her. Further, though the petitioner, along with her brother, is a director, shareholder and authorised representative of an entity, 'A', however, the respondent has not filed any complaint against the said entity. In view thereof, the petitioner has hardly any role to play qua the cheque involved in the instant dispute. Thus, the petitioner ought not to have been made an accused in the complaint by the complainant. More so, whence no vicarious liability can be fastened upon the petitioner. The scheme of the Act is such that the same is silent regarding taking cognizance against a person, other than the drawer of the cheque. [Para 10]

If the cheque in question is returned unpaid on account of the conditions mentioned under section 138, such person alone is liable to be prosecuted for the offence under section 138. The same is apparent from the phraseology "such person shall be deemed to have committed the offence" used in section 138. Proceedings and prosecution can only continue against the drawer of the cheque as the penal provisions have to be strictly construed as they are. It is, thus, that nobody barring the drawer of the cheque can be held criminally liable otherwise. It is trite law that penal provisions should be construed strictly and the emphasis is on the words, "such person" which relates to the person, who has drawn the cheque in favour of the payee [Para 11]

In view of the aforesaid, the instant petition is allowed and the complaint filed by the respondent/complainant against the petitioner and the other accused under section 138 is quashed qua the petitioner, i.e. accused no. 2 [Para 13]

admittedly, the appellant is not a drawer of the cheque and she has not signed the same. The respondent served a legal notice upon the petitioner and her brother. However, the petitioner and her brother failed to make the payment within the stipulated period. Hence, the petitioner proceeded with filing of a complaint under section 138.

Petitioner filed instant petition under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 seeking to quash said complaint. The petitioner contended that the she had been frivolously arrayed as an accused in the complaint and that the cheque from which the complaint case emanated, was neither drawn by the petitioner nor was issued from her bank account nor was it bearing her signatures.
